title: Pattern guide
text:
Piece
Meaning in today’s examples
Example




John
Literal characters
John 8:31


\d
A digit
Chapter or verse number


\s
Whitespace, including the nonbreaking space in this dataset
1 Nephi


[.-]
One listed character
A dot or hyphen


\.
A literal dot
The dot in an email domain


{5}
Exactly five repetitions
A five digit ZIP code


{1,3}
Between one and three repetitions
Chapter digits


+
One or more repetitions
\d+


?
Zero or one of the previous item
An optional verse range


(?:A|B)
Either A or B, without capturing a field
Two book names


(?P<book>...)
Capture and name a field
The book column


\b
Boundary between word and nonword characters
Before a ZIP code


^ and $
Start and end of a line/string in the usual single-line case
Checking a whole field
In Python, write regex strings as raw strings, such as r"\d{5}", so Python passes the backslashes to the regex engine. re.search() finds text inside a larger string. re.fullmatch() checks an entire string. re.findall() returns the matches, and pandas .str.extractall() makes a row for each captured match.

title: Pattern guide
text:
Things to test

Does the pattern match inside a longer value when it should not?
Does punctuation change the result?
Does the input contain a nonbreaking space or an en dash?
Are there two matches in one string, and are both returned?
Does the pattern capture only the intended book, chapter, and verses?

The citation pattern in this lesson describes recognizable text. It does not verify that a chapter or verse exists. The email example similarly finds common shapes without covering every valid address.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text: Last week, we built cleaning pipelines that keep the original data and record which rules produced the cleaned values. Today we will describe families of strings when values vary in predictable ways.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Today’s question
How can a short pattern describe ZIP codes, phone numbers, email addresses, or a simple scripture reference? How can we tell when it matches too much or misses something?

title: Regular expressions: day 1

Day 1 lecture slides, with prediction questions and their answers.
Pattern guide for looking up the syntax used in class.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do

Explain how literal characters, classes, groups, and quantifiers combine into a pattern.
Distinguish finding text inside a string from checking an entire field.
Read a short regex, predict its matches, and explain a counterexample.
Write and defend a short pattern with your group at the whiteboard.

In the next class we will apply these ideas to scripture references in the supplied conference talks. The earlier combined lecture and notebooks remain in the source package as drafts while we develop that lesson.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: Review: when a pipeline meets a new value
text:
Review: when a pipeline meets a new value
Last week, our book-name column contained Matt. and Matthew. We standardized Matt. to Matthew.
A new batch contains Matt too.
Talk with a neighbor: What would you change? What must you keep if some rows were already processed under the earlier rule?

An exact replacement works here because we have a small set of known values in a book-name field. We should not replace every occurrence of Matt in a whole talk.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Today’s problem
What if the number and placement of characters vary?
84043              84043-4820
801-555-0142       801.555.0142
tom@byu.edu        tom7@byu.edu
John 8:31          Alma 34:32
We need a way to describe the strings we want to find, rather than list them one at a time.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: A regex describes a set of strings
text:
A regex describes a set of strings
Alma 7:12 is one value. The pattern Alma \d+:\d+ describes many:
Alma 7:12     ✓
Alma 34:32    ✓
John 8:31     ✗
The book and punctuation stay fixed. The chapter and verse can change. Here \d stands for a digit, and + means one or more of the preceding item. We will work through those pieces before asking you to build a pattern.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
How we build larger patterns
A regex is made from a few types of instructions:



Instruction
What it lets us describe




Exact text
A fixed book name or punctuation mark


A choice
One allowed character or one allowed word


Repetition
A chapter with one, two, or more digits


Position
The beginning of a field or a word boundary



Putting instructions next to each other describes their order. We will learn the notation for each one in the next few examples.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: Searching and checking a whole field
text:
Searching and checking a whole field
re.search() finds a pattern inside a string. re.fullmatch() checks whether the entire string fits.
Our pattern is the literal text "cat". We wrap each result in bool() so the answer is True if there is a match and False otherwise. What will these three checks return?
import re

bool(re.search("cat", "The cat slept"))
bool(re.fullmatch("cat", "The cat slept"))
bool(re.fullmatch("cat", "cat"))
Predict with a neighbor, then compare with the next slide.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Check: search versus fullmatch
search("cat", "The cat slept")     → True
fullmatch("cat", "The cat slept")  → False
fullmatch("cat", "cat")            → True
We used bool() to ask whether a match exists. A search can succeed even when the whole field does not fit the rule.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Literal characters and the dot
Most characters match themselves. Some have special meanings.
r"byu.edu": the dot matches almost any character.
r"byu\.edu": the escaped dot matches a literal period.
The r tells Python to pass the backslash to the regex engine. We will write patterns as raw strings from here on.
With a neighbor: Which pattern accepts byuXedu? Which accepts byu.edu?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Check the dot
values = ["byu.edu", "byuXedu"]
for pattern in [r"byu.edu", r"byu\.edu"]:
    print(pattern, [bool(re.fullmatch(pattern, v)) for v in values])
byu.edu   [True, True]
byu\.edu  [True, False]
Escaping changes a special character back into the literal character.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Character classes choose one character
[.-] matches one dot or hyphen. A range such as [A-Z] matches one capital letter.
We can combine ranges: [A-Za-z0-9] matches one letter or digit. We will use that in the email exercise.
r"801[-.]555"   matches   801-555   and   801.555
Inside [ ], a dot usually has its ordinary meaning. Outside, . is a wildcard.
Predict: Would [.-] match the two-character string .- as a whole field?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
A negative character class
[^aeiou] means one character other than a lowercase vowel.
[bool(re.fullmatch(r"[^aeiou]", x)) for x in ["a", "b", "7"]]
[False, True, True]
It also accepts 7. “Not a vowel” is broader than “a consonant.”

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Useful shorthand classes



Pattern
One matching character




\d
digit


\s
whitespace, including many spaces that look ordinary


\w
word character, including letters, digits, and _


\D, \S, \W
the corresponding opposites



\w is convenient, but it may include characters your task did not intend. In Python, it can also include Unicode letters.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Quantifiers change how many



Pattern
Number of repetitions
Example




\d{3}
exactly 3
801


\d{2,4}
2 to 4
12, 8421


\d+
at least 1
7, 343


\d*
0 or more
"", 77


u?
0 or 1
color, colour in colou?r



A quantifier acts on the item immediately before it. That item can be a character or a class. On the next slides, we will make a whole group count as one item.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Groups choose whole alternatives
(?:red|blue) car allows red car or blue car.
[(v, bool(re.fullmatch(r"(?:red|blue) car", v)))
 for v in ["red car", "blue car", "red truck"]]
[('red car', True), ('blue car', True), ('red truck', False)]
(?: ... ) groups a choice. | separates the alternatives. We will use a named capturing group tomorrow when we need an extracted column.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: A class and a group are different
text:
A class and a group are different



Pattern
Its choice




[cd]
one character, c or d


(?:cat|dog)
one word, cat or dog



Predict: Does [cat|dog] match the whole word cat? Why might it still find something inside cat with re.search?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: Check the class and the group
text:
Check the class and the group
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"[cat|dog]", "cat")))
print(re.search(r"[cat|dog]", "cat").group())
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"(?:cat|dog)", "cat")))
False
'c'
True
[cat|dog] still consumes one character. For whole words, choose between groups of characters.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Pause: what is being repeated?
Compare these patterns on the whole string hahaha!:
r"ha+!"       # repeat the a
r"(?:ha)+!"   # repeat the group ha
Think, then pair: Which one matches? What string might the other match instead?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Check the quantifier’s scope
[(p, bool(re.fullmatch(p, "hahaha!")))
 for p in [r"ha+!", r"(?:ha)+!"]]
[('ha+!', False), ('(?:ha)+!', True)]
ha+! accepts haaa!. (?:ha)+! accepts hahaha!.
The parentheses determine what the + repeats.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Positions are different from characters



Position
Meaning in today’s examples




^
start of the string


$
end of the string


\b
boundary between a word and a nonword character



These symbols do not consume a character. A word boundary can occur next to punctuation, not only next to a space.
For a whole field, re.fullmatch() often states our question more directly than adding ^ and $.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Read and decipher
First think alone, then compare with a partner. Put each pattern into words. Give an example it accepts and one it rejects.

r"\bcat\b"
r"\b\d{5}\b"
r"^[A-Z][a-z]+$"

For #2, what would re.search return from 84043-4820?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
section: Read and decipher: discuss the answers
text:
Read and decipher: discuss the answers








Pattern
Reads as
Example match




\bcat\b
the word cat
cat!, but not bobcat


\b\d{5}\b
a five-digit token
84043 in 84043-4820


^[A-Z][a-z]+$
a capitalized word with more lowercase letters
Kerby, but not KERBY



Which result might be misleading? A match to the first five digits does not establish that the entire field is a plain five-digit ZIP.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Whiteboard challenge
Divide into four groups. If there are more than four groups, repeat A through D.

Write a short regex without Python quotes for your group’s whole-field rule.
Check both accepted examples and the rejected example mentally.
Write the pattern on the board. Explain each piece and propose a new test that could challenge it.

5 minutes to work, 7 minutes to share. Wait for each explanation before viewing the solution slides.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Board discussion
As each group writes its rule, everyone else should ask:

Which piece makes the rejected example fail?
What new value would you test?
Does your rule look for part of a string, or check the whole field?

Different patterns may fit the examples. We can compare how they behave on an unseen value.

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Group A: ZIP
One possible answer: \d{5}(?:-\d{4})?
84043        → True
84043-4820   → True
84043-482    → False
The optional group contains the hyphen and the four digits.
New test: Would it accept a five-digit number that is not an assigned ZIP?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Group B: phone
One possible answer: \d{3}[-.]\d{3}[-.]\d{4}
801-555-0142   → True
801.555.0142   → True
8015550142     → False
New test: It also accepts 801-555.0142. Is a mixed separator acceptable for our task?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Group C: campus email
One possible answer: [A-Za-z0-9]+@byu\.edu
tom@byu.edu    → True
tom7@byu.edu   → True
tom@byuXedu    → False
New test: It rejects first.last@byu.edu. How would the rule change if that address appeared in our data?

title: Regular expressions: day 1
text:
Group D: citation
One possible answer: (?:John|Alma) \d+:\d+
John 8:31     → True
Alma 34:32    → True
Mosiah 3:19   → False
New test: What happens with John 8:31–32? A partial match can be mistaken for a complete citation.

Explain r"[A-Z][a-z]{2,}" in ordinary language.
